textbook_segments.title: Thinking about 'Think of a Number' Tricks

periods.activity_title: Why Does the Trick Always End the Same Way?

textbook_items_in_class.description: How would you change this game to make the final answer 3? What about 5?
Find the dates if the final answers are the following: (i) 1269 (ii) 394 (iii) 296 — decode each result using the date-encoding trick.

homework.description: Try to devise your own 'Think of a Number' trick.

time_bands.activity: Open by asking students to think of any number, add 5, double the result, subtract the original number, then subtract 10. Collect several students' answers; every answer is the original number. Challenge students to explain in words — not numbers — why this keeps working regardless of the starting value.

Introduce the variable x as a stand-in for the unknown starting number and trace each step of the five-step trick algebraically, writing expressions on the board. Students mirror the steps in their notebooks. Guide the class to see that x cancels, leaving a constant — connecting the algebraic simplification to the pattern they just observed.

Figure it Out, section 6.2 p.136 ("How would you change this game to make the final answer 3?..."). Students work in pairs, adjusting the constant offset in the trick so the result shifts from 2 to 3, then to 5, using the same algebraic framework.

Introduce the two-variable date-encoding trick from section 6.2. Walk through how multiplying M by 100 and adding D after offsets embeds both values. Students then attempt Figure it Out, section 6.2 p.137 ("Find the dates if the final answers are the following: (i) 1269 (ii) 394 (iii) 296...."), decoding each answer by subtracting 165 and reading off month and day. Discuss how algebra acts as both a decoder and an inventor of such games.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often treat the variable x as a placeholder for a specific number they have not yet found, rather than as any number simultaneously — watch for students who write x = 5 after the trick and then claim the result is specific to 5. The date-encoding section rewards those who notice that 100M + D is like writing M and D side by side in a number; naming that observation explicitly builds intuition for the decoding step.

periods.activity_title: Building and Breaking Pyramids with Algebra

textbook_items_in_class.description: Use the same rule to fill these pyramids: (a) base row 6, 2; (b) base row 3, 4, 3; (c) base row 5, 4, 5, 0 — fill all missing cells upward.
What about filling in the numbers in this pyramid? Where do we start? Top is 60, bottom-left is 12, bottom-right is 8, and the middle bottom cell is unknown.
What is the relationship between the numbers in the bottom row and the number at the top? Investigate for pyramids of two and three rows using letter-numbers.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 6.3 p.140
textbook_items_in_class.description: Without building the entire pyramid, find the number in the topmost row given the bottom row in each case: (a) 4, 13, 8; (b) 7, 11, 3; (c) 10, 14, 25.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 6.3 p.140
homework.description: If the first three Virahāṅka-Fibonacci numbers are written in the bottom row of a three-row number pyramid, fill in the rest. What numbers appear? Is the top a Virahāṅka-Fibonacci number?

time_bands.activity: Draw a three-row pyramid on the board with base entries 3, 5, 2. Ask students to fill the pyramid upward using only the rule that each cell equals the sum of the two cells below it. Collect the top value and confirm, then pose: what if one base entry were unknown?

Figure it Out, section 6.3 p.138 ("Use the same rule to fill these pyramids: (a) base row 6, 2; (b) base row 3, 4, 3; (c) base row 5, 4, 5, 0...."). Students work individually, filling all three pyramids. Quickly debrief (b) to surface the pattern that middle-row entries reflect base sums.

Figure it Out, section 6.3 p.138 ("What about filling in the numbers in this pyramid? Where do we start? Top is 60, bottom-left is 12, bottom-right is 8...."). Students set up three equations using c for the unknown middle base entry and solve. Discuss why going backward requires algebra even when going forward does not.

Figure it Out, section 6.3 p.139 ("What is the relationship between the numbers in the bottom row and the number at the top?..."). Students replace base entries with letter-numbers a, b, c and derive that the top equals a + 2b + c. Record this general formula prominently.

Figure it Out Q1, section 6.3 p.140 ("Without building the entire pyramid, find the number in the topmost row given the bottom row in each case: (a) 4, 13, 8; (b) 7, 11, 3; (c) 10, 14, 25."). Students apply the formula a + 2b + c directly, bypassing full pyramid construction. Compare speed with the earlier fill-upward method.

periods.teacher_notes: A frequent error is adding all three base entries with equal weight rather than doubling the middle; emphasise that b is counted twice because it feeds two second-row cells. Having established the forward rule through the concrete examples in this unit, the generalisation to letter-numbers is a natural next step rather than an abstraction imposed from outside.

periods.activity_title: Algebra Unlocks Grids and Optimises Products

textbook_items_in_class.description: Suppose you are told that the sum of a 2×2 calendar grid is 36. Can you find the 4 numbers in the grid?

In the following grids, find the values of the shapes and fill in the empty squares: (a) 3×3 grid with squares and circles, row sums 27 and 21; (b) 3×3 grid with circles and diamonds, row sums 18 and 15.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 6.5 p.144
textbook_items_in_class.description: Fill the digits 1, 3, and 7 in □□ × □ to make the largest product possible.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 6.5 p.144
textbook_items_in_class.description: Fill the digits 3, 5, and 9 in □□ × □ to make the largest product possible.

homework.description: Create your own calendar trick. Choose a grid of a different size and shape.

time_bands.activity: Draw a 2×2 block of consecutive calendar dates starting at a. Label the four entries a, a+1, a+7, a+8. Ask students to add all four and simplify algebraically; record 4a + 16. Then pose Figure it Out, section 6.4 p.141 ("Suppose you are told that the sum of a 2×2 calendar grid is 36. Can you find the 4 numbers in the grid?"). Students solve 4a + 16 = 36 for a and write out all four dates.

Introduce the Algebra Grids subsection: rows of symbols where each row sums to a given value. Students tackle Figure it Out, section 6.4 p.142 ("In the following grids, find the values of the shapes and fill in the empty squares: (a) 3×3 grid with squares and circles, row sums 27 and 21; (b) 3×3 grid with circles and diamonds, row sums 18 and 15."). Guide students to assign a variable to each shape and write equations, then solve by substitution or elimination.

Transition to section 6.5. Present digits 2, 3, 5 and ask students to list all six arrangements of □□ × □ and compute each product. Students group results by multiplier and eliminate clearly inferior options, arriving at two finalists for discussion.

Work through the algebraic proof comparing the two finalists using expanded forms, showing which term drives the difference. Students then apply the proven rule to Figure it Out Q1, section 6.5 p.144 ("Fill the digits 1, 3, and 7 in □□ × □ to make the largest product possible.") and Figure it Out Q2, section 6.5 p.144 ("Fill the digits 3, 5, and 9 in □□ × □ to make the largest product possible."), predicting answers before computing to test their understanding of the general rule.

periods.teacher_notes: In the grid puzzles, students sometimes treat a symbol's value as different across rows; emphasise that a given shape holds the same value everywhere in the grid. For the largest-product section, the common error is placing the largest digit in the tens place of the two-digit number rather than as the multiplier — the algebraic comparison is the tool that resolves the intuition once and for all.

periods.activity_title: Proving Divisibility Rules with Place-Value Algebra

textbook_items_in_class.description: Can you work out what happens if a > b? (In the digit-reversal difference trick, when the original number is larger than its reverse.)

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 6.6 p.145
textbook_items_in_class.description: In the digit-reversal trick, what is the quotient when you divide by 9? Is there a relationship between the two numbers and the quotient?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 6.6 p.145
textbook_items_in_class.description: Instead of finding the difference of the two 2-digit numbers and their reverse, find their sum. Observe examples (31+13=44, 28+82=110, 12+21=33). Is the sum always divisible by 11? Justify using algebra.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 6.6 p.145
textbook_items_in_class.description: Consider any 3-digit number abc (100a + 10b + c). Form bca and cab by cycling digits. Add all three. Justify using algebra that the sum is always divisible by 37. Is it also divisible by 3?

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 6.6 p.146
homework.description: A mother is 5 times her daughter's age. In 6 years' time, the mother will be 3 times her daughter's age. How old is the daughter now?

time_bands.activity: Write a two-digit number on the board (e.g., 73) and its reverse (37); ask students to find the difference. Repeat with 85 and 58, then 42 and 24. Students notice the differences are 36, 27, 18 — all multiples of 9. Introduce place-value notation: a two-digit number with tens digit b and units digit a is 10b + a, and its reverse is 10a + b.

Derive algebraically that (10b + a) − (10a + b) = 9(b − a). Work through Figure it Out, section 6.6 p.145 ("Can you work out what happens if a > b?...") and Figure it Out Q1, section 6.6 p.145 ("In the digit-reversal trick, what is the quotient when you divide by 9?..."). Students observe that the quotient equals the difference of the two digits, confirming the algebraic structure.

Figure it Out Q2, section 6.6 p.145 ("Instead of finding the difference of the two 2-digit numbers and their reverse, find their sum. Observe examples (31+13=44, 28+82=110, 12+21=33). Is the sum always divisible by 11? Justify using algebra."). Students write (10b + a) + (10a + b) = 11(a + b), connecting the numeric observations to the algebraic proof.

Figure it Out Q3, section 6.6 p.145 ("Consider any 3-digit number abc (100a + 10b + c). Form bca and cab by cycling digits. Add all three. Justify using algebra that the sum is always divisible by 37. Is it also divisible by 3?"). Students write all three in place-value form, add them, factor the sum as 111(a + b + c) = 3 × 37 × (a + b + c), and confirm divisibility by both 3 and 37. A brief whole-class discussion names what algebra has done: converted an observed pattern into a proof that covers every possible three-digit number simultaneously.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently confuse the digit labels — writing the tens digit as 'a' for one number and then reusing 'a' for a different digit in the cyclic permutation; insist on consistent labelling from the first line of working. Having derived the two-digit divisibility-by-9 result in this unit, the jump to three digits and divisibility by 37 follows the same method of place-value expansion, which helps students see the proof as a transferable technique rather than a one-off trick.

items.section_title: Thinking about 'Think of a Number' Tricks
items.prompt: A 'Think of a Number' trick has these steps: think of a number, multiply it by 4, add 6, divide by 2, subtract twice the original number. A student claims the result is always 3, no matter what number you start with. Using algebra, justify why this claim is correct.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Let the starting number be x. After multiplying by 4: 4x. After adding 6: 4x + 6. After dividing by 2: 2x + 3. After subtracting twice the original (2x): 2x + 3 − 2x = 3. The x terms cancel, leaving 3 regardless of the starting value.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Represent each step as an algebraic expression and show that the variable cancels to leave a constant.

inclusivity.support: Let the student try the steps with two or three specific numbers first, then replace one of those numbers with x and repeat.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to modify the trick so the constant outcome becomes 7 instead of 3, and write the new set of steps.

exercise.description: How would you change this game to make the final answer 3? What about 5?

items.prompt: In a three-row number pyramid, each cell equals the sum of the two cells directly below it. The bottom row contains letter-numbers a, b, c from left to right. Derive an algebraic expression for the number at the top of the pyramid. Explain each step of your reasoning.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The second row has two cells: the left cell is a + b and the right cell is b + c. The top cell is the sum of these two: (a + b) + (b + c) = a + 2b + c. So the top of the pyramid equals a + 2b + c.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the pyramid rule twice — once to get the second row, once to combine the second-row cells — and simplify the resulting expression.

inclusivity.support: Suggest the student first fill a pyramid with specific numbers such as 2, 5, 3, verify the top, then repeat with a, b, c following the same steps.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask what changes if the premise is altered so each cell equals the sum of the two below it plus 1; derive the new top expression.

exercise.description: Use the same rule to fill these pyramids: (a) base row 6, 2; (b) base row 3, 4, 3; (c) base row 5, 4, 5, 0 — fill all missing cells upward.

items.prompt: Let ab represent a two-digit number where a is the tens digit and b is the units digit, so its value is 10a + b. Its reverse ba has value 10b + a. Prove algebraically that the sum of the two numbers is always divisible by 11. Then explain what the quotient tells you about the two digits.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Sum = (10a + b) + (10b + a) = 11a + 11b = 11(a + b). Since 11(a + b) has 11 as a factor, the sum is always divisible by 11. The quotient is a + b, which is simply the sum of the two digits of the original number.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Write both numbers in place-value form, add them, and factor the result to reveal 11 as a common factor.

inclusivity.support: Pair the student with a peer and ask them to verify with two numerical examples before writing the algebraic proof.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask what happens if instead of a two-digit number you use a three-digit number abc and its reverse cba — is the sum always divisible by 11? Investigate and explain.

exercise.description: Can you work out what happens if a > b? (In the digit-reversal difference trick, when the original number is larger than its reverse.)

items.prompt: A 2×2 block of dates is taken from a calendar. The top-left date is some number a; the other three dates are a+1 (top-right), a+7 (bottom-left), and a+8 (bottom-right). The sum of all four dates is 52. Find the value of a and write down all four dates.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Sum = a + (a+1) + (a+7) + (a+8) = 4a + 16. Setting 4a + 16 = 52 gives 4a = 36, so a = 9. The four dates are 9, 10, 16, and 17.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Label the top-left entry a, express all four cells algebraically, set the total equal to 52, and solve the resulting linear equation.

inclusivity.support: Provide a blank 2×2 grid and ask the student to write the expression for each cell in terms of a before summing.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to work out the rule for a 2×3 calendar grid (entries a, a+1, a+2, a+7, a+8, a+9) and find all six dates if their sum is 87.

exercise.description: Suppose you are told that the sum of a 2×2 calendar grid is 36. Can you find the 4 numbers in the grid?
